title: The vow and the fruit out of season
hook: a mother gives her unborn child to Allah, and an old guardian finds fruit that shouldn't be there

segments.voice: Yesterday, the end of Yusuf, and his words to the brothers who sold him: forgive one old thing, out loud. Did you let one old thing go? Today, a new story. Day sixty-nine.

A woman is expecting a child, and she makes a promise before the baby is even born. She tells Allah: whatever is in my womb, I give it to You, set apart for Your service. In her world, that meant a son, a boy raised to serve in the house of worship. And then the baby comes, and it's a girl. You can almost hear her surprise in the Qur'an. My Lord, I've given birth to a girl, she says, and the Qur'an adds that Allah knew best what she had delivered. She keeps the vow anyway. She names her daughter Maryam, and asks Allah to protect her and her children from Shaytan. This is how the Qur'an begins the story of Maryam: with her mother.
screen: `A PROMISE BEFORE THE BIRTH.` → `IT'S A GIRL.` → `HER NAME IS MARYAM.`

segments.voice: The Qur'an calls her mother simply the wife of 'Imran. It doesn't give her a name; later tradition calls her Hannah. And the whole family gives its name to a surah: Al 'Imran, the family of 'Imran, the third chapter. Here's what happens next. Allah accepts the girl with a beautiful acceptance, the verse says, and makes her grow up well. And an old man named Zakariyya becomes her guardian. Maryam lives and prays in a small room in the place of worship, a mihrab. The same word now names the niche in a mosque's wall that shows which way to pray. And every time Zakariyya goes in to see her, he finds food there. Food he didn't bring. So he asks her, in Pickthall's old English: “O Mary! Whence cometh unto thee this (food)?” Where does this come from? And the girl answers, simply: “It is from Allah. Allah giveth without stint to whom He will.” Without stint. In Arabic, bi-ghayri hisab: without counting, without reckoning, not measured out on a scale. Early commentators said Zakariyya found summer fruit in winter, and winter fruit in summer. The verse itself only says food, so that detail is theirs, not the text's. Now notice who teaches whom. The old guardian, the man of prayer, asks the question. The girl gives the answer. And one more thing worth knowing: commentators point out that Maryam is the only woman the Qur'an calls by her own name. A whole surah, the nineteenth, is named for her. Muslims honor her as one of the best women who ever lived.
screen: `THE WIFE OF 'IMRAN KEEPS HER VOW.` · `A MIHRAB: THE ROOM OF PRAYER.` · `WHENCE COMETH UNTO THEE THIS?` · `NAMED, WITH A SURAH OF HER OWN.` · then, large: `ALLAH GIVETH WITHOUT STINT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice a gift that came from nowhere. Sit, and breathe. Go back over the last week and look for something you didn't plan and didn't earn. A text from an old friend. A parking spot. A stranger's kindness. A song at the right moment. Something that was simply there when you walked in, like fruit in Maryam's room. Hold it for a moment. If you pray, you can say alhamdulillah for it. If not, just let yourself be surprised by it again. The bell holds the time.
Bi-ghayri hisab, without measure: how Maryam said her food came, when Zakariyya found what no one had brought.

Your line: from allah, without measure. Today, when something good arrives that you didn't plan, stop and ask Maryam's question: where did this come from? Tomorrow, the old guardian prays. Day sixty-nine.

howItsDone: Muslims read the story of Maryam's birth in Surah Al 'Imran and honor her as one of the best of women; some use her answer, 'it is from Allah', as a way of receiving unexpected good.

original.note: Arabic, Qur'an 3:37: without reckoning, without measure.

trapdoor: what you thought: a miracle story about fruit.
what it means: a mother keeps a vow even when the child isn't what she expected, and the girl is fed by Allah without measure.
what a scholar hears: hisab is counting, accounts, reckoning; bi-ghayri hisab, without reckoning. and mihrab, her room, became the name of the prayer niche in mosques.
